item.title: 'Generational rage': Young Europeans fight to be heard. [ dawn ]
item.description:
From blockaded schools in Rome to tent camps in Madrid and street protests in France, young people across Europe are turning their anger on a political class they say is not listening.

Their demands vary, but they are united in wanting to make their often marginalised voices heard, sometimes even with radical methods in the face of heavy-handed policing.

“We are fighting and taking our future in our hands,” said Damiano Fusa, 18, a student at Rome’s Cavour high school, the first to be occupied in a wave of student takeovers that has spread across the Italian capital.

“We’re not represented by anyone,” Fusa told AFP, criticising both Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s hard-right coalition and previous centre-left governments for cutting education funding and ignoring young people’s needs.

Hundreds of thousands of high school and university students have rallied in France, Italy, Spain and other European countries in recent weeks, with some protests descending into violence.

Governments have largely focused on restoring order, with France imposing partial curfews and Italy deploying soldiers, responses protesters say obscure their demands and could make things even worse.

“Politicians are responding in ways that are completely disconnected from reality, completely absurd,” said Luis Marques, a 19-year-old psychology student in Lisbon.

Students are demanding action on soaring rents, more spending on education instead of defence and more job opportunities for young people.

But experts say the unrest reflects a broader sense among many young Europeans that they have been shut out of politics and sidelined.

“These young people do not just feel like they do not have a place in politics, they feel they are not being heard at all,” said Geoffrey Pleyers, president of the International Sociological Association.

Rosario Forlenza, a professor at Rome’s Luiss University, called it a “European generational revolt” rooted in a social and economic crisis “to which politicians cannot give a substantive response”.

“Young people are a minority of the population that is shrinking and so their social, economic, cultural, political and electoral weight is becoming ever more irrelevant,” he said.

‘Inspiring other people’

The anger has been particularly palpable in France and Italy, where fresh demonstrations are planned for Saturday.

“People are very angry, they’ve had enough. Working hard all day and still not being able to fill up their shopping cart,” a 20-year-old student who gave his name as Eddy told AFP at a protest in Bordeaux last weekend.

“Will smashing everything change anything? I think it can be a jolt to wake up the politicians. We don’t know what else to do to make ourselves heard. The ballot box? We don’t believe in it anymore,” he said.

Protest movements across Europe are increasingly drawing inspiration from one another, and even looking to youth-led movements further afield in places like Bangladesh, India and Nepal.

In Italy, one student slogan last week urged protesters to “do as in France”, while shared symbols, including the Jolly Roger pirate flag, have become common across youth rallies.

Marcos Navarro, 22, a laboratory quality-control technician from Madrid, said protesters across Europe were meeting to share tactics.

“They’ve come to ask us: ‘How did you do it? How do you organise yourselves?’ We’ve already exchanged ideas,” said Navarro, who has been camping with hundreds of others in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square since September to protest housing costs and evictions.

Ayla Herrero, a 26-year-old anthropologist helping at the camp’s infirmary, said it was “inspiring for us to know that we’re inspiring other people, that it doesn’t just stay here”.

‘Not acceptable’

Concern about the rise in military spending in Europe following the Russian invasion of Ukraine has also been a rallying point.

Nikos Mavroudis, a 17-year-old high school student in Athens’ Exarchia neighbourhood, said the money could be better spent on his school, where chunks of plaster are falling.

“It’s not acceptable for classrooms to be dangerous,” said Mavroudis, who hopes to become a cook and plans to move elsewhere in Europe to “countries where things are better”.

At Rome’s occupied Morgagni high school, where students have barricaded entrances with desks, protesters pointed to the crumbling infrastructure as evidence of neglect.

An 18-year-old, who did not want to be named, said the media and politicians in Italy were focusing too heavily on looting and vandalism by some protesters.

“It turns hatred against the students who are victims of this system,” he said.

Asked about the violence, Sabrina Brizzola, 24, coordinator of the Italian University Students’ Union, said organisations like hers should “organise and channel this generational rage”.

“We have shared concerns, even if our ways of protesting differ,” she said.

item.title: Little care for healthcare. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A recent report documenting 7,500 patients waiting for radiotherapy due to a shortage of treatment facilities and capacity at National Institute of Cancer Research and Hospital (NICRH) is deeply concerning.
Every little delay can allow a disease to progress, reduce the chances of recovery, and place an even greater burden on families already struggling to cope, making this a matter of life and death.
The situation becomes more troubling when we consider how many Bangladeshis seek treatment abroad because they lack confidence in, or access to, adequate medical care at home.
However, travelling overseas is not a realistic option for most citizens. The costs of treatment, travel, and accommodation are prohibitive, while visa restrictions, the need for medical attendants, and the urgency of treatment create additional barriers.
This is not something to be taken lightly. Immediate action must begin with making the most of existing resources. The government should assess the availability and operational status of radiotherapy machines across public hospitals, repair non-functional equipment, and extend operating hours where staffing and safety permit.
Patients waiting for treatment should be registered in a centralized system and referred to facilities with available capacity. Partnerships with private hospitals could also help provide subsidized treatment to patients who cannot afford private healthcare.
Public hospitals must receive adequate funding, while transparent procurement and maintenance systems should prevent expensive equipment from remaining unused.
Cancer care, and indeed good healthcare in general, must not become a privilege reserved for those who can afford to cross borders. The government has a responsibility to ensure that citizens can access timely, quality treatment within their own country.
Promises of better healthcare mean little when patients spend their most critical days waiting. Every day lost is a day that some patients may never get back.

item.title: Prioritizing the rule of law. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The latest findings from the World Justice Project (WJP) Rule of Law Index 2026, which places Bangladesh at an abysmal 123rd out of 143 countries, should serve as an urgent wake-up call.
While the improvement from 125th last year is positive, and potentially shows that we are heading in the right direction, this marginal, fractional improvement does not change our reality, which remains humiliating.
That Bangladesh continues to trail behind several African nations, including Kenya, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe, and is languishing near the bottom of regional and global governance metrics shows that there is little to be proud of for us. Instead, it is time for some much needed humility, and the need to get to work.
There is no denying that there has been a structural decay when it comes to ensuring fundamental rights and civil justice in recent years. While minor gains were logged in governmental constraints and regulatory enforcement, fundamental rights plummeted to 133rd globally, placing Bangladesh among the lowest-ranked nations for protecting basic human freedoms.
Similarly, civil justice ranked a dismal 132nd, demonstrating that access to effective remedies and impartial dispute resolution remains an empty promise for ordinary citizens.
When a country's judicial and legal frameworks fail to guarantee basic security, equity, and civil protection, it is the entire nation and its people that bear the ramifications.
We cannot take comfort in sluggish, incremental movements when systemic rot continues to paralyze our institutions. We must recognize and address the bureaucratic inertia, selective legal enforcement, and political interference that have corroded the judiciary and law enforcement bodies.
Talk of reform continues to fall on deaf years, yet comprehensive, aggressive institutional reforms remain more urgent than ever before. Bangladesh will never reach its potential as a nation without restoring public trust. For that, the rule of law must apply equally to all.

item.title: Debates that never happened. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Imagine scrolling through YouTube at midnight and meeting a split screen. Sheikh Hasina sits on one side, Jamaat Ameer Dr Shafiqur Rahman on the other, and the title promises a face-to-face clash on Khaled Muhiuddin’s talk show.
More than 352,000 viewers watched it, and thousands argued in the comments as if they had witnessed live television. They had not. No studio, no host, and no debate ever existed.
A second video was bolder still. Its caption said Hasanul Haq Inu was speaking live right after leaving jail while Prime Minister Tarique Rahman listened. In reality, editors arranged old footage to mimic a real-time exchange, and Inu has been in custody since 2024.
Both clips are cheapfakes: No artificial intelligence, just cutting, a split screen, and a trusted program’s borrowed look.
Neither case is an accident. A recent study by FactWatch identified around 300 similar items and then examined several platforms.
According to findings, the YouTube channel Rajnoitik Studio and the Facebook page Bangla News240 collectively published more than 300 fabricated shows that accumulated roughly 517K followers.
The fabricated broadcasts typically target sensitive political topics, elections, or public controversies to shape public opinion or push partisan agendas. The casting is telling. Fabricated statements and deepfakes regularly target key political leadership.
Why does the talk-show format work so well? A studio duel squeezes messy politics into a contest anyone can follow, and the host lends borrowed authority. A reel then strips away the channel behind it, so viewers see a clip, not its source. People struggle most when fakes wear a news format.
By combining psychological manipulation with media impersonation, these AI-generated “talk shows” and deepfakes weaponize local cultural sensitivities to shift public opinion. A single deepfake is easy to ignore, but hundreds of them create an illusion of reality.
If a viewer scrolls and sees others echoing the same political talking point, they begin to believe that the entire country feels that way.
One fake show persuades a few people; a hundred of them feel like a national mood.
Prof Sumon Rahman, founding editor of FactWatch, has warned that confirmation bias and timing can confuse even media-literate viewers.
This is a tactic of manufactured majoritarianism. A report reveals that nearly 30,000 fake reactions were purchased from four click farms. They cost roughly Tk 120 to 200 per thousand, and some arrived within minutes. A review of 263 posts counted 885,811 reactions, 62% of them “haha,” and at least 19,708 came from bot-like profiles.
“How artificial intelligence and synthetic reality shaped Bangladesh’s 2026 election,” a study concluded that coordinated narrative manipulation had become a structural feature, introduced with Bangladesh’s first AI-saturated election, where seeing was no longer believing.
No single mastermind appears in the record. Instead, several actors overlap. The click-farm probe found politically aligned clusters moving in tandem, yet it did not examine official party links. The administrators of those talk-show channels never answered the questions.
Some operators work alone. Anthropic’s September threat report, relayed by bdnews24, described one operator in Gaibandha who rotated 29 AI accounts over about 16 months and produced roughly 1,500 fake headlines. The company found no evidence that the Awami League ran or funded the network.
Others are plainly commercial.
FactWatch exposed a counterfeit Prothom Alo page with an invented interview with Abdullah Abu Sayeed that steered readers toward a trading platform; meanwhile, the Daily Star documented 52 deepfake videos and 31 pages offering fake Family Cards for likes.
Consequently, “who” is less a mastermind than a marketplace.
FactWatch’s data offers a before-and-after picture. In its 2024 election study , video made up 71.9% of 157 unique hoaxes, and only three, or 1.9%, were deepfakes.
By 2026, another analysis of 72 AI-manipulated cases found that 49% invented what leaders did or said, and 28% used AI-edited photocards to fake quotes.
After Osman Hadi was shot on December 12, 2025, fact-checkers documented within two days fake photocards in the names of RTV, Kalbela, BBC Bangla, and Amar Desh, an AI image of a suspect, and an AI clip in which a hand grips a man yet belongs to no one.
A widely shared photograph of Shadik Kayem with the suspect was synthetic, yet BNP’s Ruhul Kabir Rizvi cited it at a rally and later apologized.
For years, the standard advice has been to tell citizens to verify before sharing. That advice is sound, yet it is unfair on its own. A viewer on a bus, with a phone and little data, cannot reverse-search a split screen.
After the Cyber Security Act of April 2026, draft amendments would force platforms to remove harmful AI content, and Transparency International Bangladesh and other rights groups fear a return to Digital Security Act-style repression.
A vague takedown power is easily aimed at critics, and real journalism can also be dismissed as fake. Any rule should therefore target fraud, impersonation, and paid fake engagement, with judicial review and public reporting, rather than “misinformation” in general.
Broadcasters and newsrooms have a duty. Every outlet whose face or microphone is borrowed should publish a quick, searchable “this is not ours” notice, and should consider visible watermarks on original clips.
The click-farm evidence shows that candidates from several parties share the same bot pool. A public pledge never to buy engagement, never to circulate unverified cards, and to apologize quickly when fooled would cost nothing. Rizvi’s apology was a start; it should become a norm.
Return, finally, to that midnight scroll. The harm of a fake talk show is not only that someone believes a debate occurred.
Political factions in Bangladesh do not just create fake videos for entertainment; they use them to manufacture deliberate, high-stakes narratives.
A falsehood once believed does not stay online. It walks into real politics.
A studio that never existed can cost a few hours and a laptop. Rebuilding trust in real ones will cost far more.
Zulker Naeen is a Research Coordinator, Centre for Critical and Qualitative Studies (CQS) and Adjunct Faculty, Department of Media Studies and Journalism (MSJ), University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB). Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: The psychological wall between cultural and national identity. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It seems the city authority, in trying to do a good thing, has landed in serious trouble. In the middle of it all, there was an unwelcome tug-of-war over the portrait of the late Sanjib Chowdhury. This dramatic chain of events around the wall doesn’t only raise questions about the city authority’s judgement. It also points to a social, political, and psychological problem in Bangladesh.
Among Bangladesh’s many problems is the fact that it has two “ages.” As an independent state, Bangladesh is only 55 years old. But on the basis of the Bengali language and culture, the Bengali nation is very old. Reconciling the two should not be a problem. But religious division, and its influence on society and politics, has made this simple task difficult.
Take the wall of the Shilpakala Academy in Segunbagicha. The Dhaka city authority decided to clear hawkers from the footpath beside the road and decorate the wall beautifully. Good. They decided that, instead of using bright colours alone, they would also paint portraits of some of the country’s eminent figures. Better still.
Trouble broke out over whose portraits. The question arose: What do we mean by “country,” and even if these figures are eminent, are they really “ours?” And what exactly do we mean by “ours?”
The country is only 55 years old, so finding “eminent” figures is also hard. It may sound a little harsh, but it isn’t untrue. In any society, it takes time for a poet, writer, musician, politician, or intellectual to be counted as eminent.
Today there are many people, living or dead, who are enormously popular. But it will take them a long time, a very long time, to reach the eminent or classic level.
From Shakespeare to Nazrul
In the Western world, this matter doesn’t create much controversy. Britain’s The Beatles and America’s Elvis Presley are undoubtedly the most popular modern musicians in the West.
But when portraits are placed on currency or in nationally important places, the West goes back to its classical era, whether in music, literature, or painting. Many people dislike Britain’s former prime minister Winston Churchill. But his huge statue in Parliament Square, for leading Britain in the Second World War, and his picture on the £5 note don’t cause much controversy. (Though far-left youths occasionally smear red paint on the statue, because in their eyes Churchill was a symbol of racist imperialism.)
The vast difference between the two categories, eminent and popular, is not understood by many, or they understand it but pretend not to.
This difference does not disrespect popular figures. Rather, it tells their followers that their time will come too. But before that, we must see whether the work of those who are popular today will still be relevant 100 years from now. Will it still be read in schools and colleges, as the literature of William Shakespeare, Rabindranath Tagore, or Kazi Nazrul Islam is taught today? To cross the boundary of popularity and reach the classical level, a person’s work must survive even a hundred years after their death.
By that measure, Sanjib Chowdhury’s portrait does not belong beside Rabindranath’s or Nazrul’s. But that wall is a fitting place for Begum Rokeya or Jibanananda Das, because they are truly eminent. Yet an injustice has also been done to Sanjib Chowdhury. If there was a case for keeping him on the wall, why was he removed? By putting him up once and then taking him down under criticism, the authority has insulted the memory of the late artist, which perhaps did not occur to them.
The deeper problem of the wall
If the city authority had wished, it could have decorated one or two entire walls with portraits of popular writers, musicians, and actors. Beside Sanjib Chowdhury, portraits of popular but late figures such as Ayub Bachchu, Azam Khan, Humayun Faridi, Al Mahmud, Shamsur Rahman, Farida Yasmin, and Zahir Raihan could have found a place.
But even then, problems would have arisen. There are many popular figures, and a fresh controversy would begin over why those left out were not included.
But this wall has exposed an even deeper problem. 55 years after independence, the debate over the country’s and the nation’s self-identity has still not stopped, as we have once again been made to see plainly.
Art, literature, music, and cinema are all part of a nation’s cultural life. Language and cultural heritage play the main role here, although at different stages of history, religion has had a big influence in building that heritage.
When people in Bangladesh search for the roots of their culture, when they want to remember the names and work of their own eminent figures, national borders will not be able to hold them back.
Bangladesh’s culture did not begin after the birth of the independent state. In search of the country’s luminaries, many names will come up who are Bengali in heart and soul but whose work was completed before independent Bangladesh was born.
To find the eminent figures of Bangladesh’s cultural world, one has to look beyond not only 1971 but the twentieth century. There, which side of the new border someone’s birthplace fell on after the 1947 partition of India should have no place in the debate.
The greatest Bengali BBC list
That 1971 left a huge mark on the hearts of the people of Bangladesh can be seen from a 2004 experience at BBC Bangla.
BBC Bangla’s plan was to make a series of programs on eminent figures through a listener poll. Listeners were asked: In your opinion, who is the greatest Bengali of all time? And not just one name. It was decided to make a list of 20 and produce a radio feature on the life of each eminent person.
The list shows that, at least, BBC Bangla radio listeners did not take the present national borders into account in choosing the “greatest Bengali.” Rising above religious and political divisions, they looked for their own people.
While fixing the broadcast date, an unexpected surprise came up. Counting the days, it turned out that March 26 to April 14 was exactly 20 days. That meant the series on “the greatest Bengali of all time” could begin on Bangladesh’s Independence Day and end on Bengali New Year’s Day, Pohela Boishakh. What could be a more fitting time for this series?
In the list drawn up from the listeners’ votes, first place went to Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and second to Rabindranath Tagore. Then came Kazi Nazrul Islam, A K Fazlul Huq, Subhas Chandra Bose, and Begum Rokeya Sakhawat. After them came Jagadish Chandra Bose, Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani, Raja Ram Mohan Roy, Titumir, Lalon Fakir, Satyajit Ray, Amartya Sen, the martyrs of 21 February, Dr Muhammad Shahidullah, Swami Vivekananda, Atisha Dipankar, Ziaur Rahman, and Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy.
This poll was not without controversy. Some Islamist newspapers found a “Brahminical conspiracy” behind it. A far-left editor saw in the publication of the list an attempt to boost the Awami League’s movement against the then BNP government. But one of my colleagues at the BBC was only surprised.
Achala Sharma, then head of the BBC’s Hindi service, who had learned Bengali only to read Sarat Chandra’s books, expressed her surprise to me. “Why didn’t Rabindranath come first?” she asked. I gave her my analysis. “If this poll had been held 40 years ago, Rabindranath would undoubtedly have been chosen as the greatest Bengali. But in these 40 years, Bangladesh was born, and as the architect of the Bengalis’ first independent state, Mujib’s place in the listeners’ minds has moved above Rabindranath’s.”

item.title: The quiet hours we lost. [ tbsnews ]
When survival becomes a debt-financed affair. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Economic distress does not always announce itself through factory closures, unemployment queues, or empty markets. Sometimes, it reveals itself through a quieter transformation: Families continue working, shops remain open, salaries arrive on time, yet ordinary incomes no longer cover ordinary lives.
Parents reduce food purchases, postpone medical treatment, borrow from relatives, and exhaust savings to maintain familiar routines. The appearance of normality conceals a deterioration in economic security.
Bangladesh’s latest household survey offers a troubling account of this contradiction, suggesting that for millions of people, survival increasingly depends on money they have not yet earned.
According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics’ Living Standard Survey 2025, 47.42% of households borrowed money to meet daily expenses during the preceding year. The proportion reached 51.91% in rural areas, compared with 40.19% in urban areas and 32.11% in city corporation areas.
These figures deserve attention not simply because borrowing is widespread, but because of its reported purpose. Loans taken to expand businesses or finance education may generate future returns. Loans taken to purchase necessities indicate that present consumption has become difficult to sustain through existing income.
The survey identifies the underlying arithmetic. Average monthly household income stands at Tk 33,513, while expenditure reaches Tk 35,311, creating a monthly deficit of Tk 1,798. This difference may appear modest when expressed as a national average, but its implications are substantial.
The annualized gap amounts to Tk 21,576 per household, assuming the monthly deficit persists. For families already operating close to subsistence, such a shortfall can consume savings, increase dependence on informal credit, and leave little capacity to absorb emergencies. The average also conceals households whose deficits are considerably larger.
More importantly, the relationship between income and expenditure has changed. In the 2022 Household Income and Expenditure Survey, average monthly household income was Tk 32,422 against expenditure of Tk 31,500. Income exceeded expenditure by Tk 922.
The latest survey reverses that relationship. Although nominal household income has risen, expenditure has increased faster, suggesting that additional earnings have not translated into greater financial security.
The figures do not establish why every household is borrowing, nor do they reveal the distribution of deficits. Nevertheless, they identify a structural warning: Rising incomes mean little when the purchasing power they represent is insufficient to sustain consumption.
This distinction challenges a common assumption in economic debate: That an increase in nominal earnings necessarily indicates improved welfare. What matters is the relationship between income, prices, and essential needs.
If wages rise by less than the cost of food, housing, transport, and healthcare, workers become poorer in practical terms without necessarily receiving smaller pay packets. Their nominal income may increase while their real choices contract.
They can continue buying necessities only by reducing quality, sacrificing other needs or borrowing. Economic insecurity thus develops not only through income loss but also through the gradual disappearance of affordable alternatives.
Bangladesh’s wage and inflation figures reinforce this interpretation. Government data indicate that inflation exceeded wage growth for 56 consecutive months through September 2026. Meanwhile, annual wage growth slowed from 8.05% in August to 7.9% in September. These figures suggest that workers have endured a prolonged erosion of purchasing power.
However, the national averages should be interpreted carefully: Households differ in their employment, earnings, and consumption patterns, while inflation affects expenditure categories unevenly. Lower-income families are particularly vulnerable because food and other necessities absorb a larger share of their budgets, leaving less room to adjust when prices rise.
The consequences become clearer when regional differences are examined. Average monthly household expenditure is Tk 46,778 in city corporation areas, Tk 37,344 in other urban areas, and Tk 32,532 in rural areas. Yet rural households report the highest incidence of borrowing.
This apparent contradiction disappears once expenditure levels are distinguished from economic capacity. Urban households may spend more because housing, transportation, and services are expensive. Rural households may spend less because their incomes are lower and their consumption is already constrained.
Lower expenditure, therefore, cannot automatically be interpreted as greater affordability. It may instead reflect deprivation that household averages fail to capture.
The composition of expenditure also matters. Rural families devote relatively more of their budgets to food, while non-food items account for 56.7% of household expenditure in city corporation areas.
These patterns expose different dimensions of vulnerability. When food prices rise, rural households have limited scope to reduce an already essential expense. Urban families face pressure from rent, transport, education, and healthcare, costs that are often difficult to avoid.
Consequently, identical inflation rates can produce unequal hardships. Effective economic policy must account for these differences rather than treating households as interchangeable units in a national average.
Rural indebtedness also reflects differences in employment opportunities and income stability. Agricultural earnings can be seasonal, while informal employment frequently provides neither predictable wages nor protection against illness and unemployment.
Remittances support many communities, but their benefits do not reach every household. Families without stable employment, migrant earners, or adequate savings may have few alternatives when essential expenses exceed income.
Borrowing bridges the immediate gap without correcting its cause. If the next month’s earnings remain insufficient, repayment becomes another expense competing with food, healthcare, and education. What begins as temporary assistance can become a recurring mechanism for financing poverty.
This is why the distinction between productive and distress borrowing is essential. Credit can help households acquire assets, establish businesses, and improve their future earning capacity.
Borrowing for consumption is not necessarily harmful when it addresses a temporary disruption and repayment is affordable. The danger arises when loans repeatedly finance unavoidable expenditure without a credible prospect of higher income.
In such circumstances, debt does not smooth consumption across time; it transfers deprivation into the future. Interest payments may then deepen the original shortfall, while the absence of savings makes households increasingly vulnerable to economic shocks.
The wider economic environment compounds this pressure. The World Bank’s Bangladesh Development Update, released on October 6, warned that prolonged economic weakness, inadequate labour demand and persistent inflation were undermining living standards.
It projected that the national poverty rate could rise from 18.7% in 2022 to 22.5% in 2026. This is a projection, not a confirmed outcome, but it signals a serious risk.
The energy crisis adds another constraint by increasing production difficulties, reducing operating hours and discouraging recruitment. When businesses cannot expand employment, households lose opportunities to compensate for rising prices through additional earnings.
These pressures reveal a limitation in judging economic performance primarily through aggregate growth. Growth can coexist with declining household security when its benefits are unevenly distributed, employment creation is inadequate or real wages stagnate.
The survey alone cannot establish the precise contribution of each factor, but its findings, considered alongside wage and inflation data, suggest that economic recovery cannot be assessed solely by the movement of headline indicators. The decisive question is whether growth generates reliable incomes and whether those incomes preserve people’s ability to meet essential needs without sacrificing their future.
The human consequences extend beyond material deprivation. Financial insecurity forces families to make decisions that rarely appear in economic statistics. A parent may postpone a child’s education, an elderly person may delay treatment, or a worker may continue an exhausting job because losing even one month’s income would be disastrous.
Such compromises gradually diminish opportunity and dignity. Children growing up in financially strained households may inherit disadvantages through poorer nutrition, interrupted education, and reduced access to healthcare. Household debt can therefore transmit present economic weakness into future inequality, making recovery more difficult across generations.
The government must respond with a combination of immediate protection and structural reform. Controlling inflation requires credible macroeconomic management, stronger competition in essential commodity markets and action against practices that unnecessarily increase prices.
Employment policy must encourage productive investment, reliable energy supply, and the creation of decent-paying jobs. Wage adjustments should reflect actual living costs, particularly for vulnerable workers, while targeted social assistance should protect households unable to absorb further shocks.
Better income and expenditure data would also help identify which groups face the largest deficits and whether interventions improve their circumstances.
The Ninth National Pay Scale provides one immediate policy context because the National Pay Commission commissioned the BBS survey to inform its recommendations. Public employees’ purchasing power deserves consideration, but cannot resolve a wider crisis affecting private-sector workers, informal labourers, and rural households.
Poorly calibrated increases could also create additional fiscal pressures without addressing the causes of inflation. The challenge is to protect workers’ real incomes while strengthening productivity, employment, and price stability. A credible response must recognize that household welfare depends on both what people earn and what their earnings can actually buy.
Ultimately, the most revealing measure of economic progress is not simply how much money enters a household, but whether that money provides security. When nearly half of households report borrowing for daily expenses, the issue extends beyond individual financial management.
It raises questions about wages, employment, prices, and the distribution of economic opportunity. Debt used to build a future can represent investment; debt repeatedly used to purchase necessities signals that the present is becoming unaffordable.
Bangladesh must confront this distinction before borrowing becomes an ordinary condition of family life, and financial insecurity becomes an inherited feature of poverty.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.description:
Star Australian fast bowler Megan Schutt was suspended for two matches on Thursday for breaching prescription medication rules.

The 33-year-old, who was a standout in Australia’s recent one-day series against Bangladesh, apologised for “failing to meet the standards” expected of her.

Cricket Australia said in a statement she breached “requirements under the Sports Science and Sports Medicine guidelines with regard to prescription medication”.

“This relates to a single incidence which occurred while out of competition and was not for performance enhancing purposes,” it added.

“We will continue to provide appropriate support to Megan and reinforce the standards and responsibilities expected of everyone representing our game.” Her two-match ban will see Schutt miss Thursday’s third and final T20 against New Zealand and the Adelaide Strikers’ opening game of the Women’s Big Bash League later this month.

“I fully accept the penalty handed down and apologise for failing to meet the standards expected of me,” said Schutt, who has played 114 ODIs and 126 T20s for Australia.

item.title: Projects must be completed on time. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The stalled Tk9.33 crore drainage project in Shibganj, Chapainawabganj, is another example of how unfinished commitments can undermine the very purpose of development.
The 2.1-kilometre drainage project, intended to address waterlogging, has remained stalled for six months, with around 300 metres still unfinished. Disputes with local residents over the land required for construction have prevented work from proceeding.
Meanwhile, it is the everyday public that are left to navigate damaged roads, accumulated rainwater, and disrupted business activities.
A development project is only as valuable as the benefits it ultimately delivers. Yet, in Bangladesh, we continue to see public works announced, funded, and initiated, only to be left incomplete for months or even years.
Of course, disputes over land and residents’ concerns cannot simply be dismissed. Authorities must listen to affected people, explain the project’s requirements, and seek fair, practical solutions.
However, negotiations cannot become an excuse for indefinite inaction. Municipal officials must take responsibility for resolving the impasse and establish a clear, publicly communicated deadline for completing the remaining work.
This case raises questions about how public projects are planned and managed. Potential obstacles, including land disputes, should be identified before construction begins. Feasibility assessments, consultations with residents, and contingency plans must be integral to project preparation, rather than treated as matters to address after work has stalled.
Accountability must also extend to implementation. Authorities should regularly publish progress updates, monitor contractors against agreed timelines, and explain delays when deadlines are missed. Where obstruction occurs, officials must pursue lawful solutions instead of allowing an entire project to languish.
Every delayed project imposes costs on ordinary citizens, who lose time, income, and access to essential services while waiting for improvements that may never arrive on schedule.
Development must therefore be measured by whether the intended benefits reach the people. It's time to recognize that starting projects is a responsibility, but finishing them is an obligation.

item.title: For harmony and worship. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The peaceful conclusion of this year’s Durga Puja celebrations across Bangladesh offers a powerful affirmation of our enduring ethos of communal harmony and pluralism.
From vibrant pandals packed with devotees to our leaders visiting numerous sites and being with the people to even the warm solidarity shown by the diplomatic community joining festivities nationwide, this year’s celebrations demonstrated the unbreakable bond of shared heritage.
Indeed, leadership at the highest levels, from Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visits to local pandals to President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir’s greetings urging youth to champion inclusivity, underscored a unified national commitment to protecting the rights, dignity, and security of every citizen, regardless of their religious background.
Crucially, law enforcement agencies reported no evidence of orchestrated conspiracies or malicious plots disrupting the festival. While there were some incidents that soured the experience for some in the country, what we take away from this week is that when the state enforces rigorous security and vigilance to thwart sectarian troublemakers, peace prevails.
For years, bad actors and dark political forces have sought to weaponize communal friction, manufacturing fear, and exploiting fault lines to fracture society - forces that persist to this very day. Yet, the overwhelming response of the public continues to be one of collective rejection toward those who peddle hatred and division, and long may it continue.
Diversity is not merely a demographic reality in Bangladesh but the bedrock of our national identity. As the festivities conclude, the collective resolve witnessed during Durga Puja must not fade.
The government, civil society, and ordinary citizens must maintain this unwavering vigilance, ensuring that secularism and mutual respect remain uncompromised throughout the year.
We must continue to foster an environment and be a nation where minorities are protected, traditions are honoured, and communal harmony is fiercely defended against any voice that seeks to tear us apart. This is the sign of true development.

item.title: The politics of othering. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
While the state repeatedly pledges to uphold law and order, insecurity among minority communities remains palpable. Police records from 2025 documented 645 incidents involving members of minority groups, classifying 71 as communal and 574 as ordinary criminal offenses.
The Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council reported 257 incidents of communal violence in just the first six months of 2026, resulting in 44 deaths across 40 separate attacks.
While statistical discrepancies exist, the underlying reality is undeniable. Ensuring the safety, dignity, and equal rights of religious minorities remains an urgent national priority.
Against this backdrop, an even deeper question has emerged into public debate: Does the state have the authority to determine the religious identity of its citizens?
The issue reached a head on August 15, 2026, when the International Majlis-e-Tahaffuz Khatme Nabuwwat Bangladesh convened a National Ulama-Mashayekh Conference. The gathering culminated in a nine-point demand, chief among them that the Ahmadiyya community be legally declared a "non-Muslim minority."
Other demands included prescribing the maximum legal penalty for insulting Islamic sanctities, barring Tablighi leader Maulana Saa'd from entering the country, prohibiting his followers from holding the annual Ijtema, and banning the group Hizb-ut-Tawhid.
Jamiat Ulama-e-Islam Bangladesh President Maulana Ubaidullah Farooq has called on Hefazat-e-Islam to announce a parliament siege program this November if the government does not declare Ahmadis (Qadianis) non-Muslims. Similar calls were voiced at a Khatme Nabuwwat conference late last year.
These demands go beyond routine theological disagreement. They raise fundamental questions regarding religious identity, individual liberty, and the limits of state power.
Attending seminars organized by the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community in Bangladesh, conversing with their representatives, and reviewing their publications reveal a faith rooted in Islamic fundamentals alongside distinct theological perspectives.
The Ahmadiyya community firmly identifies itself as Muslim. Members uphold core Islamic principles: Affirming the absolute oneness of God, honouring the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), and following the Holy Quran.
At the same time, Ahmadi theology diverges from mainstream Sunni and Shia doctrines on specific theological points. Most notably, the community believes that Mirza Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian was the Promised Messiah and Mahdi , and holds a distinct interpretation regarding the death of Jesus (PBUH).
Despite theological differences with broader groups, the community emphasizes building harmonious relations across society.
Guided by their global motto, "Love for all, hatred for none," Ahmadi Muslims in Bangladesh actively promote peace, interfaith dialogue, and mutual understanding.
This philosophy of openness extends to their places of worship. The Ahmadiyya community welcomes anyone regardless of background or belief to visit their mosques across the country.
Representatives express a warm readiness to engage in polite conversation and address questions from anyone curious to learn about their faith and traditions directly.
While mainstream scholars view these doctrines as incompatible with orthodox Islamic theology, a critical line is crossed when a theological verdict is converted into a legal identity imposed by the government.
At the international level, Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights explicitly guarantees the right to freedom of thought, conscience, and religion, including the freedom to manifest one's faith publicly or privately.
Crucially, Islamic scripture and tradition also address the gravity of judging another person's faith. Surah An-Nisa (4:94) in the Quran warns believers: "Do not say to one who offers you peace (Salam), ‘You are not a believer.’"
The verse cautions against hasty declarations and urges careful verification.
This is reinforced by a well-known Hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari , where Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) stated: "Whoever prays like us and faces our Qibla and eats our slaughtered animals is a Muslim and is under Allah's and His Apostle's protection (Bukhari, Kitabus Salat:384)."
Furthermore, while a tradition in Jami' at-Tirmidhi speaks of the Ummah eventually dividing into 73 groups (Tirmidhi:2640), it raises a poignant question: When theological differences inevitably arise, who holds the authority to decide which group is legally Muslim and which is not?
Pakistan offers a sobering case study of what happens when the state steps in to settle theological disputes.
In 1974, Pakistan constitutionally declared Ahmadis to be non-Muslims . Subsequent penal laws criminalized basic Ahmadi religious expressions, making it illegal for them to publicly identify as Muslims or use standard Islamic terminology. Minority Rights Group has extensively documented how codifying theological rulings into state law institutionalized discrimination and fueled systemic violence.
Bangladesh has already seen warning signs of such rhetoric spilling over into physical harm. In March 2023, a violent attack on an annual Ahmadiyya convention in Ahmadnagar, Panchagarh, left people dead, scores injured, and homes and properties burned.
Sociologist Pierre Bourdieu framed this dynamic through the concept of " symbolic violence ," a phenomenon where a dominant group uses institutional power to impose definitions and labels on a weaker group. When theological critiques are backed by state power, symbolic violence easily turns into physical disenfranchisement.
There is a vital distinction between theological debate and state-enforced identity. Religious scholars have every right to argue that certain doctrines conflict with mainstream Islam. However, the state’s duty is entirely different: Its obligation is to safeguard constitutional rights, maintain public order, and ensure equal citizenship for all.
This debate is not merely about one specific community; it touches on the foundational principles of the republic.
Who ultimately holds the right to define a citizen’s religious faith -- the individual, a dominant religious group, or the government?
How Bangladesh answers this question will define its commitment to human rights, freedom of conscience, and the rule of law.
The state need not become an arbiter of religious truth. Its fundamental responsibility is far simpler: To protect the life and security of every citizen while ensuring that theological disagreements never become an excuse for exclusion, discrimination, or violence.
Dilawar Hossain is a Research Associate at the Brac Institute of Educational Development . Rezwana Zaman Diya is a development professional.

item.title: The women are divine. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Among Bengali idol-makers, there is an old, informal belief, passed along by word of mouth - that a Durga is incomplete unless a handful of earth from the doorstep of a sex worker is mixed into her clay. The explanation given is that “a man who enters that house leaves his virtue at the door, so the ground there becomes pure.”
Whether or not every workshop still follows it, the idea deserves a slow reading. The goddess cannot be completed without the woman’s soil, and the woman herself cannot be admitted to the festival. The earth is holy; the person is not.
This October 2026, as pandals lit up from Khulna to Old Dhaka, the belief is worth asking about, because it states, in clay, how this society thinks about women.
Psychology has a name for the split. Freud’s 1912 essay, On the Universal Tendency to Debasement in the Sphere of Love , described men who can desire only a woman they have debased, and cannot desire the one they respect. It later became known as the “Madonna-whore” complex.
His diagnosis was about men, but the habit of mind is far older than his essay. Women were sorted into two boxes: “Pure” and “the fallen,” with nothing allowed in between.
Literature has always known it. Nathaniel Hawthorne branded Hester Prynne with a scarlet letter; Thomas Hardy subtitled Tess of the d'Urbervilles , “A Pure Woman” and then punished her for being human.
Our own Sarat Chandra gave us the sharpest Bengali version in Devdas. Paro, the respectable, forbidden girl, and Chandramukhi, the courtesan in whose house Devdas drinks himself to ruin.
Nazrul saw it too. In his poem Barangana , he stunned society by addressing a prostitute as “mother,” and asked who had the right to spit at her. He pointed out that the heroes and sages of our own myths had unmarried or “fallen” mothers. More than a century on, we still have not caught up with our national poet.
In life, and in death
Bangladesh is among the few Muslim-majority countries where prostitution is legal for adult women who hold a certificate, but the law is ambiguous, leaving sex workers vulnerable to harassment and prosecution.
In July 2014, around 1,500 women were forced out of the 200-year-old Kandapara brothel in Tangail. A High Court judgment in 2000 had called such evictions unconstitutional, but it was never implemented.
Newspaper reports have noted that sex workers are denied food, clothing, shelter, health, and education. When sex workers go to the police after being raped, they are ridiculed. Why? Because people cannot imagine a sex worker being raped. Many mothers send their children away, believing life outside the brothel will be harder because of stigma.
Even death is a denial. Locals refuse to organize funerals for sex workers, neighbours did not bathe her, and a local imam refused to lead her prayers. The only place available for sex workers’ bodies was a cremation ground.
In February 2020, Hamida Begum became the first sex worker in Daulatdia to receive a formal Islamic funeral. Until then, their bodies were often tossed into unmarked graves or the river.
Afterwards, the imam who led the prayers said he would not do it again, because villagers and shopkeepers had criticized him. The Sex Workers Network is still demanding equal burial arrangements.
The pedestal and the fall
A woman who must stay pure carries the family’s ijjat , its honour, in her body. And a stain, even one inflicted by someone else, turns the Madonna into the whore.
Look at who is made to hide. According to the Bangladesh Mahila Parishad, 786 women and girls were raped or gang-raped in 2025, up from 516 the year before while Ain o Salish Kendra counted 749 cases. Police headquarters recorded 21,939 cases of violence against women and children in 2025.
Between January and May this year, ASK recorded at least 118 children raped and 17 killed . In five recent high-profile cases, the victims were targeted by neighbours, relatives, or acquaintances.
Behind each number is a person who, in a society that has split women into goddesses and whores, now holds the “whore” half. Rape is generally branded as a stain on a woman’s chastity and honour more than as a crime against her body, which shifts the focus from the accused to the victim.
The victim is so heavily stigmatized that perpetrators use the crime itself to silence her. Society collectively ostracizes the victim and her family, which is why most rapes go unreported. Abusers justify the crime by blaming the victim; if she takes the blame, the culprit feels he did nothing wrong.
The same soil
In the soil story, men shed their virtue at a woman’s threshold and the ground holds it. In life, men shed their guilt at a woman’s threshold and she holds it. We bow to the clay goddess and then cannot bear the woman.
A society that calls women its mothers, then cannot bury them, cannot hear them, and makes the raped one hide her face while the rapist is shielded, has not forgotten reverence. It has made reverence a way to keep women in their place.
The idols are immersed. But the women are still at their doorsteps, and many are still hiding their faces. Divine in theory, dirty in practice.
Shuchi Binte Shahjalal is a member of the Editorial and Op-Ed team at the Dhaka Tribune and looks after the Trib Z and Arts & Letters pages.

item.title: OpenAI expands ChatGPT ads to 26 more countries, including Pakistan, in bid to boost revenue. [ dawn ]
item.description:
OpenAI said on Wednesday it was expanding advertising on ChatGPT to 26 more countries, including Pakistan, ​bringing the total to 89 as ‌the AI company beefs up its advertising business to boost revenue ahead of a potential initial public ​offering.

The company said in August its ads ​business had reached an annualised revenue run ⁠rate of $1 billion.

OpenAI began testing ads in ChatGPT ​in the US earlier this year, and ​more than 100,000 advertisers have since run campaigns on the platform, the company said.

The expansion adds 14 more ​Latin American countries, including Argentina, Chile, Colombia ​and Peru, following launches in Mexico and Brazil.

Ads are also launching in markets across Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia, including Nigeria, South Africa, Serbia, Ukraine, Cambodia, Bangladesh and Pakistan.

Advertisers can access ​ChatGPT ads ​in the ⁠new markets through technology partners, or get self-service access via Ads Manager ​on the company’s platform.

Ads will appear ​only ⁠on ChatGPT’s Free and Go plans, while Plus, Pro and Enterprise subscriptions will remain ad-free.

In ⁠September, ​OpenAI introduced AI-powered tools for ​advertisers and began testing business-sponsored agents with select US advertisers.

item.title: The making of Bangladesh’s architectural excellence. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The Royal Institute of British Architects’ (RIBA) prestigious International Prize has been awarded to Karupannya’s Green Field factory in Rangpur.
Designed by the soft-spoken and unassuming architect Bayezid Khondker and his practice, Nakhsabid Architects, this is yet another architectural feather in our cap. And this is not the first time a building from Bangladesh has won the award.
Friendship Hospital in Satkhira, designed by architect Kashef Chowdhury, won the prize in 2021.
Since the prize’s inception in 2015, there have been five winners, two of them from Bangladesh.
The Karupannya factory was selected from four shortlisted projects, two of which were from Bangladesh, the other being the BRAC University campus in Dhaka, designed by WOHA, an architectural practice based in Singapore.
The shortlist was drawn from 34 projects recognised in the RIBA International Awards for Excellence 2026.
Louis Kahn lecturing at BUET in the 1960’s. Photo: Collected
The list included another project from Bangladesh: the Zebun Nessa Mosque, designed by Saiqa Iqbal Meghna of the practice Morphogenesis.
Bangladeshi architects have won numerous notable international awards for their work.
These include the prestigious Aga Khan Award for Architecture.
Kashef Chowdhury and Marina Tabassum won the award separately in 2016, followed by Saiful Haque in 2019, and Khondaker Hasibul Kabir and Suhailey Farzana, Rizvi Hassan, Khwaja Fathmi and Saad Ben Mostafa in 2022.
Marina Tabassum won again in 2025, setting a record by becoming a two-time recipient of the award.
Other projects in Bangladesh that have received this award include the Grameen Bank Housing Project and the Bangladesh National Parliament building, designed by Louis I Kahn.
Bangladesh has the second-highest number of projects to have won this award, after Iran. Another recipient was Bangladeshi structural engineer FR Khan for his design of the Hajj Terminal at Jeddah Airport.
Bangladeshi architects have also received countless international awards and recognitions over the years.
These include awards from the Commonwealth Association of Architects (CAA), the JK Cement Awards, the International Union of Architects (UIA), and ARCASIA, among others. Listing all the awards and their recipients would leave little room to discuss the actual subject of this article.
Given that Bangladesh is a small country with about 5,000 registered architects, compared with approximately 150,000 in India, 6,000 in Pakistan, 130,000 in the United States and 28,000 in the United Kingdom, it can confidently be said that we have performed better than our neighbours, including India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Malaysia.
The Architecture building at BUET. Photo: Collected
Why is this so? Is there something we have that others do not? Is it genetic? Is it training and education? Or is it passion? It is difficult to pinpoint any single reason or even draw up a definitive list of reasons.
If one were to examine the background that has produced good architects in Bangladesh, several possible explanations might emerge. There is no empirical evidence, data or research to support these explanations. They are simply observations about the culture of architecture in the country.
We have Muzharul Islam, the pioneering modern architect of the country and the region, and examples of his world-class architectural projects, built from shortly after Partition through to the 1980s. In him, we also have an architect who set an example not only through outstanding buildings but also through high ethical standards and devotion to the profession, not to mention his eloquent, sophisticated and articulate personality.
Bangladeshi architects, almost without exception, recognise him as a ‘guru’ and look to his high standards as an example to follow. His creations, including the Charukala Institute, the Dhaka University Library, the NIPA building and the two universities, continue to be landmarks and sources of inspiration. For students, visiting some of his buildings is almost like a pilgrimage.
Then there is the National Parliament building complex, designed by Louis I Kahn. The Parliament building itself is recognised as one of the hundred most influential buildings of the last century.
Muzharul Islam was instrumental in bringing Kahn, an internationally recognised master architect, to this country. Islam believed that our country should have an exemplary work by a renowned architect of the time, just as India had Le Corbusier, and convinced the government to engage Kahn. This was Islam’s gift to the younger generation of architects. Architects and students continue to study this remarkable example and draw inspiration from it.
In the 1960s, quite a few internationally renowned architects worked here. Paul Rudolph designed several buildings at Mymensingh Agricultural University. Constantin Doxiadis designed the Teacher-Student Centre (TSC) at Dhaka University, the Home Economics College and the BARD complex in Cumilla, among others. Muzharul Islam and Stanley Tigerman jointly designed five polytechnic institutes.
There were others, such as Robert Bouighey, Richard Vrooman and Daniel Dunham, who were less widely known but designed buildings that inspired our architects. These included Kamalapur Railway Station, halls of residence at BUET and Dhaka University, the Faculty of Architecture and Planning at BUET, and buildings at Rajshahi University, among others. These buildings are excellent examples of tropical modernism and provide valuable lessons for architects.
Friendship Hospital, Satkhira. Photo: Courtesy of Kashef Chowdhury
The Department of Architecture at the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET), then known as the East Pakistan University of Engineering and Technology, introduced an undergraduate program in architecture in 1962.
It was initially established by a group of American teachers from Texas A&M University. They included Richard Vrooman, who was the first dean and the architect of the faculty building. The building is still in use and remains cherished by students and alumni alike. Other teachers included Daniel Dunham and Walden, among others.
They taught a small group of students for several years until Bangladeshi teachers who had been sent abroad returned to take over around 1967–68.
From the very beginning, the department developed a ‘culture’ in which architecture was treated with the utmost seriousness as a profession. There was an almost sacred devotion to the subject, something approaching religious conviction. Students and teachers alike were deeply committed.
The building itself helped foster this culture, with its spacious corridors, large studios and an open ground floor supported by columns, now known as the ‘plinth’. It became a place for serious discussions and arguments.
I have not encountered this kind of passion in any other school, although I have taught at several institutions abroad and visited many others.
Let me cite a small incident that exemplifies this almost religious devotion.
A younger colleague, who was also a former student, and I were teaching architectural graphics to freshmen. My colleague was explaining how to set up their drawing sheets on the table.
He said, “First, go and wash your hands carefully with soap and dry them.”
When the students had done so and returned to class, he explained how the drawing sheet had to be aligned with the parallel bar and fixed to the table with tape, and how pencils needed to be sharpened—preferably by hand with a blade rather than a sharpener, then further sharpened using grade 0 sandpaper and dipped into Styrofoam to remove graphite granules.
Once that was done, he said, “Now go and wash your hands again.”
When they returned, he told them, “Now approach your work as if you are performing ‘ebadad’, meaning prayer.”
The entire ritual of washing one’s hands twice before approaching the task with the devotion of prayer had to be followed. Such was the culture.
The carefully designed admission process ensured that only students with a genuine interest in architecture were admitted.
There was a separate admission test for architecture, with 80% of the questions assessing creative and drawing skills and the remaining 20% covering mathematics. The mathematics questions were exceptionally difficult, going beyond what students had learned at the HSC level, and candidates did not have to pass that section separately to qualify.
I believe this was quite deliberate, ensuring that students could not gain admission solely on the strength of their mathematical knowledge.
The result was that students who genuinely wanted to study architecture and possessed drawing and artistic skills were admitted, although the competition was intense. The studios appeared to have a more artistic than technical orientation.
Unfortunately, that admission system was discontinued in 1999, and there is now a common admission test for the whole of BUET. Eight architecture faculty members resigned in protest and left.
Now, this department was housed within a technical university where the majority of programs were in engineering. In technically oriented universities around the world, architecture programs tend to have a technical inclination. But at BUET, architecture was artistic.
Moreover, the faculty building occupied its own separate space, away from engineering.
Students and faculty members from other disciplines often regarded architecture as a less serious subject than their own. Architecture was ridiculed, and there were taunts about architecture students doing little more than drawing trees and similar things.
The subject was even referred to as “yarki-tecture”, with yarki being the Bangla word for joke or banter.
This no longer happens. Bangladeshi architects have proved themselves and have received more international accolades than members of any other profession in the country.
Such was the devotion to and seriousness about architecture.
Meanwhile, the country’s economy began to grow, creating opportunities for architects to showcase their work. Architecture has become a popular profession, and there are now more than 30 architecture programs across the country.
There may be other reasons why Bangladesh produces such good architects, but I cannot say with certainty what they are.
Today, apart from the architects who have already won awards, there is an emerging generation of talented young architects producing excellent work.
This tradition of good architecture will continue.
The author is the Dean of the School of Architecture and Design at Brac University and the founder of its architecture program. He is a graduate of BUET and has also taught there.
